summary: Young children (ages 5–6) distinguish flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes. This is genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). A central, curriculum-supported approach is handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space in every direction — supported by a dimensional discriminator ('is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card?') and the explicit twin-pair vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube, and loosely triangle/pyramid, since a pyramid has triangle faces). A paper cut-out can itself be picked up and has a slight thickness, so 'can you pick it up?' is not the reliable test; treat the card as a stand-in for an ideal flat shape. Instruction and experience, not age alone, help move children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality.
misconceptions: Applies a flat (2-D) name to a solid object — calls a ball 'a circle', a cube 'a square', a cone 'a triangle' (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023; Nurnberger-Haag).
Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups the round ball with the round circle because both 'look round' (van Hiele visual level).
Confuses a drawing of a solid with the solid itself — treats a cube drawn on paper as 'solid' because of its name.

activities.title: Hold-and-turn sort with real solids and flat cut-outs
steps: Gather a mixed set the child can handle: a ball, a cube-shaped box, a pyramid, a tin, a cone, beside a paper circle, square and triangle. The paper shapes can also be picked up and have a tiny thickness, so treat each as a stand-in for the ideal flat shape it represents.
Pick up and turn each object over in your hand. Ask: is it round or thick in every direction so it takes up space (solid), or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card (flat)?
Sort the set into two hoops or bins labelled 'flat' and 'solid'.
Include a cone and other less familiar or non-prototypical solids, not only balls and boxes.
Go on a 'shape hunt' around the room to find more solids (a tin, a ball, a box) and say why each takes up space in every direction.
Name the twin pairs aloud as you sort: circle/sphere, square/cube, and triangle/pyramid (a pyramid has triangle faces, though its base may be a square).
activities.insight: A flat shape has length and width but (ideally) no thickness, and a paper card stands in for it; a solid takes up space in every direction (length, width and height). 'Round like a circle' is not the same as flat — a ball is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere, not a circle. (For the adult: because a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness, 'can you pick it up?' is not the real test — ask whether the shape takes up space in every direction.)

activities.title: Build a solid from flat paper (pop-up)
steps: Start with a flat paper net (an unfolded pattern of joined flat shapes) and fold/assemble it into a solid (e.g. a pop-up cube or pyramid).
As the solid takes shape, touch and count its faces, edges and corners (vertices).

Compare the finished solid, which now takes up space in every direction, with the flat sheet you started from. Name the solid and the flat shapes of its faces: a cube has square faces, and a pyramid has triangle faces (a square pyramid also has a square base). The unfolded sheet (the net) is several joined shapes, not one square or triangle.
activities.insight: A solid takes up space in every direction and has faces you can feel and count, whereas the flat paper it came from only lies in a plane — the same name family splits into a flat word and a solid word.

activities.title: Spin-to-compare on screen (scaffold alongside handling)
steps: On screen, spin a circle and a ball. Watch the circle thin to a line and vanish when turned edge-on, while the ball stays round from every side.
Say why: the ideal circle has no thickness, so it disappears edge-on; the ball is round every way and never flattens — it cannot be a circle, it is a sphere.
Immediately repeat with a real paper circle and a real ball in your hand, turning each to feel that the ball is round in every direction while the card is thin.
activities.insight: An ideal flat shape has no thickness and disappears edge-on; a solid takes up space from every direction. Rotating a model shows this effect, while handling a real object additionally lets the child feel the three-dimensionality directly, so the two are paired. (A real paper circle is a thin card standing in for the zero-thickness ideal.)

checkQuestion: Here is a ball, a paper circle, a cube (box) and a paper square. Sort them into 'flat' shapes and 'solid' shapes. Then tell me: why isn't the ball flat, even though it looks round like the circle?
checkAnswer: Puts the paper circle and square with the flat shapes and the ball and cube with the solids; explains that the ball is solid because it is round in every direction and you can hold and turn it and it takes up space, whereas the circle just lies flat on the paper — so the ball is a sphere, not a circle.
